title: Conjunctive queries: fast evaluation
lead: Query graphs and hypergraphs, acyclicity, GYO reduction and Yannakakis evaluation.

sections.title: Structural restrictions on queries
sections.html:
General CQ evaluation is NP-complete in combined complexity, but restrictions on query structure can make it tractable. The source distinguishes graph-based and hypergraph-based restrictions.

The query graph connects variables that occur together in an atom. The query hypergraph represents each atom by a hyperedge containing its variables. A high-arity atom is therefore represented directly rather than only through pairwise edges.

Bounded treewidth restricts the graph; bounded hypertree width restricts the hypergraph. Acyclic CQs form an important hypergraph-based class. A cycle in the ordinary graph does not by itself establish hypergraph cyclicity.

PDF pp. 1–5

sections.title: Join trees and acyclicity
sections.html:
A join tree has nodes labelled by query hyperedges. Every hyperedge is represented. For each variable, all nodes whose labels contain that variable must form a connected subtree: the running-intersection property.

A hypergraph is acyclic if it admits such a tree. Connectivity for each individual variable ensures that consistency of values can be propagated through adjacent relation pairs.

The source contrasts a triangle of pairwise edges with a structure containing an additional encompassing hyperedge. The latter can have a join tree even though its ordinary graph contains a triangle. Acyclicity here is the hypergraph notion.

PDF pp. 6–13

sections.title: GYO reduction
sections.html:
GYO repeatedly removes a vertex occurring in at most one hyperedge and removes an empty hyperedge or one contained in another. Apply the rules until no rule changes the hypergraph.

The hypergraph is acyclic exactly when this process reduces it to the empty hypergraph. A remaining irreducible structure witnesses failure of the test. Removal of contained edges is essential; deleting only low-degree vertices is insufficient.

The source gives a full reduction sequence and states that acyclicity testing and join-tree construction are tractable, with linear-time algorithms in the query size. The reduction is a structural test, independent of current database tuples.

PDF pp. 14–26

sections.title: Boolean evaluation by semijoins
sections.html:
The presented Yannakakis algorithm evaluates an acyclic Boolean CQ. Construct a join tree and associate each node with the database relation for its atom. Process children before their parent.

For each child C of parent P, replace P by P ⋉ C on their shared variables, after C has already been reduced by its descendants. A semijoin keeps parent tuples with at least one matching child tuple; it adds no child columns and does not multiply parent tuples.

The running-intersection property ensures that the subtree constraints are represented by the surviving tuples at each step. After all children are processed, the root records which assignments have support throughout the tree.

PDF pp. 27–35

sections.title: Decision result and output-size limits
sections.html:
For the Boolean problem, return YES if the reduced root relation is nonempty and NO otherwise. The source example ends with a surviving root tuple and therefore returns YES.

The source discusses efficient acyclic query evaluation in terms of database and query size. This does not mean that all tuples of a large non-Boolean answer can be written independently of its output size.

Full result enumeration generally adds a top-down reduction and join/enumeration work, with output-sensitive accounting. The slides’ bottom-up Boolean test should not be confused with a complete implementation that enumerates every projected answer.

PDF pp. 36–37

quiz.question: GYO reduction stops with the triangle {a,b}, {b,c}, {c,a}. What follows?
options: It is acyclic because it has three edges
It is cyclic because reduction cannot eliminate the whole hypergraph
Every possible database must be tested
No query corresponds to this structure
quiz.explanation: No variable has degree at most 1, and no edge is contained in another. The nonempty structure left by GYO reduction establishes that the hypergraph is cyclic.

source.summary: Lecture 25 introduces conjunctive-query graphs and hypergraphs, useful structural classes, join trees, GYO reduction, and Yannakakis’s algorithm for acyclic queries.

limitations: The stated time bound does not include enumerating an arbitrarily large output. This lesson focuses on the decision problem.
